newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Presidential pilot fired in Colombian drug scandal.
newsitem.headline: Presidential pilot fired in Colombian drug scandal.

text.p: The pilot of Colombia's presidential jet has been fired as part of an investigation into the discovery of more than eight pounds (3.7 kg) of heroin aboard the aircraft, officials said on Tuesday.

The "narco-jet" scandal erupted on Sept. 20 just hours before President Ernesto Samper, already tainted by allegations of links to drug barons, was due to fly to New York to address the United Nations General Assembly.

Defence Minister Juan Carlos Esguerra said Col. Jaime Bueno, who was also the commander of the Catam military air base in Bogota where the Boeing 707 was stationed, had been replaced by Col. Gonzalo Morales.

Samper said the heroin was part of a plot to further muddy his image, and local press reports pointed the finger at the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) and speculated on a joint drug-smuggling network run by top-ranking officers in the Colombian and Peruvian armed forces.

But the prosecutor's office heading the inquiry remained tight-lipped over what line of investigation it was pursuing. Its only public action was to arrest and interrogate 11 crew members and technicians, including Bueno.
A spokesman said on Tuesday that no other arrests were planned at the moment and denied reports that Samper would be called to give evidence.
"It is a very remote possibility that the president would be called. That would only occur if his name was linked to the heroin find," he said.

Bueno's dismissal was the result of an internal investigation by the Colombian Air Force which a spokesman for the prosecutor's office said should not be interpreted as an indication that he was directly to blame for the drug stash.
U.S. Ambassador Myles Frechette was forced to issue a terse statement over the weekend denying that DEA agents had tampered with the presidential jet before Samper's scheduled departure.
Air force commander Gen. Hector Hernando Gil likewise denied any of his men were involved in drug-smuggling.
The Catam base has periodically been the centre of narco- scandals since 1984 when military intelligence alleged air force officers were running an arms-and-cocaine smuggling ring.

Since then drug cartel kingpins stole a jet from the base, more than a ton of dynamite was found in a junior officer's house, and cocaine and heroin were found aboard Colombian Air Force C-140 Hercules transporters on two occasions, most recently at the start of this year.

Samper largely escaped the fallout of the latest scandal to rock his administration. An anonymous tipoff just before his flight to New York spared him further international embarrassment -- he was stripped of his U.S. visa earlier this year for what the United States described as his known dealings with drug kingpins.
Last month, the DEA revealed Colombian cartels had become the main suppliers of heroin, of exceptionally high purity, to the United States.
